title: Gotchas
short: The traps that silently break correct-looking interview code.
what: A handful of Python habits produce wrong answers with no error message. Almost all come from one fact: a name points at an object, and several names, rows or calls can end up sharing the same one.
analogy: Three photocopies of a house key are still keys to one house. Paint the kitchen with one key and every key holder sees a painted kitchen.

frames.label: bad = [[0] * 3] * 3
frames.say: [[0] * 3] * 3 looks like a 3 by 3 grid of zeros. But * 3 copies a pointer to one row, not the row itself.

frames.label: bad[0][0] = 1
frames.say: Set bad[0][0] = 1 and every row changes. The three rows are one list seen three times.

frames.label: good[0][0] = 1
frames.say: Build rows with a comprehension: [[0] * 3 for _ in range(3)]. Each turn makes a new row, so one cell changes.

frames.label: def add(x, seen=[])
frames.say: def add(x, seen=[]) makes that list once, when def runs. Every call shares it, so add(2) still sees the 1.

frames.label: def add(x, seen=None)
frames.say: Fix: default to None and make the list inside, with if seen is None: seen = []. Each call starts fresh.

frames.label: nums = [2, 4, 5, 6]; remove evens in the loop
frames.say: Removing while looping shifts items left under the loop. 4 slides into a spot already visited and is never checked.

frames.label: slow or wrong
frames.say: Three more: += on a string can copy it each time, / makes a float index, and b = a copies no list.

when: Making a 2D grid or DP table
A default argument that is a list or dict
Removing items from the list you loop over
python:
bad = [[0] * 3] * 3
bad[0][0] = 1
good = [[0] * 3 for _ in range(3)]
good[0][0] = 1
print(bad, good)
def add(x, seen=[]):
    seen.append(x)
    return seen
print(add(1))
print(add(2))
nums = [2, 4, 5, 6]
for x in nums:
    if x % 2 == 0:
        nums.remove(x)
print(nums, [x for x in [2, 4, 5, 6] if x % 2], 7 / 2, 7 // 2)
cost: s += c in a loop, n times
watch: Use None as the default for a list or dict argument, then create it inside the function.
Loop over a copy (for x in nums[:]) or build a new list instead of removing as you go.
In backtracking, save res.append(path[:]), not res.append(path), or every saved answer changes later.
